title: What counts as a word: tokens, types, TTR, tokenization, normalization
summary: Distinguish lemma / wordform / type / token and compute TTR; explain Heaps' law and why TTR only compares equal-size texts; list where whitespace tokenization fails; reproduce the normalization table and give three examples of what cleaning erases.
sourceNote: Lecture 5 (Sep 8) and Lecture 6 (Sep 10) slides, J&M ch. 2.1–2.6, chance quizzes.

sections.heading: Why 'what is a word' is a real question

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Every technical choice is a linguistic claim** Before you can count words, you have to decide what a word is — and ==every answer erases something==. Is *San Francisco* one word or two? Is *don't* one? Are *Apple* and *apple* the same? Kraus's line: **'Tokenization is an analytic decision, not a neutral preprocessing step.'** Her chance-quiz questions almost all have the same shape: *true or false about a definition*, then *give one example of what a choice preserves or erases*. This chapter is that answer bank.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** 'What counts as one unit' is a live question in every data job: is a returning visitor a new *type* or another *token* of an old one? Are 'NYC' and 'New York City' one row or two? And the loudest modern version — large language models don't read words, they read tokens, so half the internet's 'why can't the AI count the r's in strawberry' complaints are this lecture wearing a new shirt. The engineers debugging those systems are answering Kraus's question with code.

blocks.body: the dictionary headword — same stem, same part of speech, same basic sense. *cat* and *cats* are one lemma.
the fully inflected surface form. *cat* and *cats* are two wordforms.
a distinct element of the vocabulary V. Whether types are counted as lemmas or wordforms is a decision.
one instance of a type in running text. Counting tokens gives n, the text length.
types that occur exactly once in a corpus. In natural text, roughly half the vocabulary is hapax.

blocks.title: Counting types and tokens; computing TTR

frames.caption: Gertrude Stein's line, split on spaces. Every word you can point at is a **token** — an instance. Count them: 8. (Kraus's slide counts the full 'a rose is a rose is a rose' line as 10 tokens with 'rose' at the start; the method is what matters.)
Now count **types** — distinct words. 'a' appears three times but is one type.
'is': two tokens, one type. That's every word accounted for. **3 types, 8 tokens.**

**Type–token ratio.** Low TTR means lots of repetition; high TTR means varied vocabulary. Stein's line is deliberately repetitive. The first line of Wikipedia's 'Rose' article scores about 0.92 — almost every word is new.

Real corpora. Notice the pattern: **the bigger the corpus, the lower the TTR**. That's not because Google's English is boring. It's because vocabulary grows slower than text (next section), so tokens outrun types. TTR is only comparable between texts of similar size — Kraus's caveat about Alice vs Moby Dick.

blocks.title: 'they sat back on their San Francisco stoop and looked up at the stars and their'
blocks.body:
How many tokens, how many types?

1. Split on spaces: 16 tokens. If *San Francisco* is one multi-word token: 15. Already a decision.
2. Types: *and* appears twice, *their* twice. 16 − 2 = 14 types. Treat *San Francisco* as one: 13. Lemmatize *stars* → *star*, *looked* → *look*? Still 13 here (no collisions), but in a longer text lemmatizing shrinks V.
3. There's no single right count. The right answer names the decisions: 'Sixteen tokens on whitespace, fourteen types as wordforms; fifteen and thirteen if multi-word place names are one token.'

blocks.prompt: Compute TTR for 'the dog saw the other dog and the other dog saw the cat'.
blocks.answer: 13 tokens. Types: the, dog, saw, other, and, cat = 6. TTR = 6/13 ≈ 0.46.

blocks.prompt: Chance quiz: separate the morphemes in *rewriting* and *undermined*. And: T/F, hapax legomena are very common in corpora.
blocks.answer: re-writ(e)-ing; under-mine-(e)d. True — around half of all types in a natural corpus occur once.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Type vs token is the working vocabulary of search engines — an index maps each *type* to the positions of all its *tokens* — and of stylometry, where TTR-family measures helped attribute the Federalist Papers and still catch ghostwriters and essay mills. Readability formulas score textbooks with these counts; fraud teams flag accounts whose TTR is eerily low, because spam repeats itself. ==When an NLP paper says 'vocabulary size |V|', it means the number of types== — and someone had to make exactly the decisions this section names to get that number.

sections.heading: Heaps' law: why vocabulary grows slowly

frames.caption: **Heaps' law.** Read it as: 'vocabulary size is some constant times the token count raised to a power less than 1.' The power less than 1 is the whole message.

lines: if β were 1:  double the text → double the types
β ≈ 0.5:  double the text → ×2^0.5 ≈ ×1.4 the types
frames.caption: A power of 1 would mean every new chunk of text brings as many new words as the first chunk. A power around 0.5 (a square root) means new words come more and more slowly — you keep seeing the same common words, and only occasionally a new rare one.

With K = 30, β = 0.5: a thousand-fold increase in text gives roughly a thirty-fold increase in vocabulary. Diminishing returns for rare words — which is why a 1-million-word corpus like Brown already has most of the common vocabulary, and why hapax legomena (words seen once) are so common: the tail never fills in.

lines: each counts as a new type unless you decide otherwise
frames.caption: The catch: typos, stretched spellings, and case variants all look like new types to a computer. Whether they *are* new types is a decision — which is what the rest of this chapter is about.

The dashed line is the world where every new page brings new words at a constant rate; the green curve is the real one — V = K·nᵝ with β near 0.5, so a thousandfold more text buys only about thirtyfold more vocabulary. The red gap is pure repetition, and it is exactly why TTR falls with length and why Alice vs Moby Dick is an unfair fight. Hover any part.
blocks.slide: Heaps' law: the curve that bends

blocks.body: **The TTR caveat (a likely midterm question)** Alice in Wonderland TTR ≈ 0.097; Moby Dick ≈ 0.080. That does **not** mean Melville had a smaller vocabulary. Moby Dick is about eight times longer, and by Heaps' law tokens grow faster than types, so its ratio *must* be lower. TTR only compares texts of similar length. To compare different lengths, use a fixed window (TTR over the first 10,000 tokens of each) or a size-corrected measure.

blocks.md: Frequency reveals things the words alone don't: register (formal text uses *however*; chat uses *lol*), speaker age, subject matter, dialect. A frequency list is the first thing a corpus linguist looks at — and ==every number in it depends on the tokenization and normalization decisions below==.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** Heaps' law is capacity planning. Search engineers use it to predict how big an index's dictionary gets at ten times the documents; ML engineers use it to size embedding tables before training. It's also the reason LLM tokenizers cap their vocabularies at roughly 50K–200K learned subwords instead of using words: ##V never stops growing, so any fixed word list eventually leaks — subword tokenization is the industry's escape hatch##. Even 'how much more data until we've seen the rare cases?' — the question every self-driving and content-moderation team asks — is a Heaps-shaped question with a Heaps-shaped answer: more slowly than you hope.

blocks.body: Breaking a continuous stream of text into meaningful units (tokens). The questions to ask: where are the boundaries? what are the minimal units? what linguistic structure does this preserve or erase?
Chinese 姚明进入总决赛 — is that 3, 5, or 7 tokens? 'Tokenization requires a theory of wordhood.' Japanese mixes four writing systems and needs a lexicon-based segmenter; Thai, Burmese, Ge'ez similar.
German *Flughafensicherheitskontrolle* (airport security check) is one orthographic word and three or four lexical ones.
*Ph.D.*, *W.H.O.* (one unit each); *$89.99* vs *$8999*; *1/25/2026*; URLs and emails. Strip punctuation and these change meaning or vanish.
*we're*, *I'm*, *don't*; French *j'ai*; Spanish *dámelo* (give-me-it). One word or two or three? NLTK splits *don't* into *do* + *n't*.

*New York City*, *father-in-law*, *back and forth*. NLTK splits them (MWETokenizer can rejoin from *your* list); spaCy splits, then recovers spans via named-entity recognition and noun chunks; Penn Treebank tags each piece and keeps the unit in the tree.

blocks.prompt: Chance quiz: T/F — it's fine to remove all punctuation when tokenizing, since punctuation doesn't tell you anything important.
blocks.answer: False. Punctuation marks conventional units (Ph.D.), encodes magnitude and currency ($89.99), carries structure (dates, URLs), and delimits sentences. Removing it changes meaning before the analysis starts.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** This section's failure list is the design brief for LLM tokenizers. **BPE (byte-pair encoding)** — what GPT-style and Claude-style models actually run on — is the industrial descendant of this lecture: it gives up on wordhood entirely and learns frequent character chunks from data, so *Flughafensicherheitskontrolle* becomes a few subwords, unspaced Chinese segments without a hand-built lexicon, and no word is ever out-of-vocabulary. The costs are this lecture's costs too: ==a model that sees 'strawberry' as two or three opaque chunks genuinely cannot count its letters==, and languages that fragment into more tokens pay more per API call. Closer to home, every search box doing CJK segmentation and every `text.split()` you'll ever regret in a notebook are the same story.

sections.heading: Normalization: what to standardize and what to keep

blocks.body: Making different surface forms comparable by mapping them to a standard representation. 'Tokenization feeds normalization.' The question is never *whether* to normalize but *which variation is noise for your question and which variation is the data*.

rows: color / colour, e-mail / email, st. / street
don't → do not, gonna → going to, yeah / yah / ya
lol, u vs you, texting shorthand
blocks.slide: The normalization table (slide 28 — shown three times)

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why the bottom rows say PRESERVE** The rows to normalize are variation that *doesn't correlate with anything linguistic* — a typo tells you nothing about the writer. The rows to preserve are variation that *is* linguistic evidence: register, dialect, identity. If your research question is about those, !!normalizing them away deletes your data!!. If it isn't, they're noise. The table isn't a rule; it's a way of asking 'what is my question?' before touching the text.

blocks.body: erases pragmatic cues: 'Excellent, another meeting 🙄' is sarcastic; without the emoji it's sincere.
erases proper-noun and category signals: *Apple* vs *apple*; German *Essen* (food, noun) vs *essen* (to eat, verb) — capitalization *is* the part of speech.
erases identity, dialect, expertise, play: 'yall be trippin lol' → 'you all are tripping' loses everything the writer chose.
collapses *Ph.D.*, *$8.99*, sentence boundaries, *tl;dr*.
is ambiguous: '1915 J St' — nineteen fifteen? one-nine-one-five? 'roll two sixty four sided dice' — 264? 2 × 64? 260 × 4?
preprocessing is technical access (strip HTML, tokenize, split sentences); annotation is linguistic interpretation (POS tags, parses, sentiment). Next chapter.

lossless shaping is reversible — the original is recoverable. Lossy is not — lowercasing, emoji removal, stemming all discard information for good. Prefer keeping the raw text and deriving normalized *views* of it.

blocks.prompt: Chance quiz: give one example of how lowercasing or removing emojis can alter or erase linguistic information.
blocks.answer: Lowercasing: *Apple* (company) → *apple* (fruit) loses the named-entity distinction; German *Essen/essen* loses noun vs verb. Emoji: 🙄 flips sincerity to sarcasm.

blocks.prompt: Is stemming lossy or lossless? Why does it matter for a dialect study?
blocks.answer: Lossy — *running, runner, runs* → *run* can't be reversed. A dialect study needs surface forms (*sittin* vs *sitting*), so stemming or spell-normalizing would erase the very variable under study.

blocks.md: **Lectures 5–6 in one paragraph.** Tokens are instances, types are distinct forms, lemmas are headwords; TTR = types/tokens and falls with length because vocabulary grows as K·nᵝ with β < 1 (Heaps). Whitespace tokenization fails on unspaced scripts, compounds, meaningful punctuation, clitics, and multi-word expressions. Normalize noise and orthography; preserve register and dialect. Every cleaning step is lossy or lossless, and every lossy step is a linguistic claim — ==name what it erases==.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** The normalization table is the honest job description of data work — most of any analytics or ML role is deciding what to clean and knowing what the cleaning destroys. Search engines case-fold so 'apple' finds 'Apple', then special-case the collisions that matter; sentiment models that strip emoji lose the sarcasm bit exactly as the 🙄 example warns; dialect-aware moderation breaks when someone upstream 'fixed' the spelling. The keep-raw-derive-views habit is the raw/staging/clean layering every data-engineering team runs. !!Cleaning you can't undo is analysis you can't revise!! — keep the original.

exercises.title: Count tokens and types — then defend the count
exercises.prompt: Text: `I can't believe it's already 5pm! I CAN'T. Time flies, doesn't it? #mood 😩` Give the token count and type count under (A) whitespace splitting with no changes and (B) NLTK-style tokenization with lowercasing. Then write two sentences on what (B) erased that a study of *register* would need.
hints: For (A), just count space-separated chunks — punctuation stays attached ('5pm!' is one token). For (B), NLTK splits 'can't' into 'ca' + "n't", separates punctuation, and lowercasing merges 'I CAN'T' with 'I can't'.
The usual error is doing only one count and treating it as *the* answer. The exercise is about how the count *changes* with the decision, and being able to say by how much.
What does 'CAN'T' in capitals tell you that 'can't' doesn't? What does the emoji do to the sentence's tone? Those are the register signals lowercasing and emoji-stripping delete.
solution: (A) Whitespace: I · can't · believe · it's · already · 5pm! · I · CAN'T. · Time · flies, · doesn't · it? · #mood · 😩 → 14 tokens. Only 'I' repeats exactly ('can't' and 'CAN'T.' differ in case and punctuation), so 13 types.

(B) NLTK + lowercase: i · ca · n't · believe · it · 's · already · 5pm · ! · i · ca · n't · . · time · flies · , · does · n't · it · ? · # · mood · 😩 → 23 tokens; types: i, ca, n't, believe, it, 's, already, 5pm, !, ., time, flies, ,, does, ?, #, mood, 😩 → 18 types.
TTR moves from 13/14 ≈ 0.93 to 18/23 ≈ 0.78 — from the decisions alone, not the text.

(B) erased emphasis (CAN'T vs can't — shouting is register), and stripping/separating the emoji loses the exasperated tone that flips the meaning of 'Time flies'. A register study needs both preserved.
exercises.why: Two people can 'count the words' in the same text and get numbers 60% apart, both correct under their decisions. Reporting the decisions with the number is what makes a result reproducible — the whole point of documentation in Lectures 7–8.

exercises.title: The TTR comparison trap
exercises.prompt: A classmate reports: 'Brown's *news* category has TTR 0.14 and *science fiction* has TTR 0.19, so sci-fi authors use a richer vocabulary.' Is the conclusion justified? What one fact would you need to check first, and what would you do instead?

choices.text: Yes — a higher TTR means more types per token, which is richer vocabulary by definition.
choices.feedback: That's the definition, but TTR falls with length (Heaps' law). If the two categories have different sizes, the comparison is meaningless.

choices.text: Not yet — check the token counts of the two categories; if they differ, compare TTR on equal-size samples (e.g. the first 10,000 tokens of each).
choices.feedback: Right. Brown's news category is about 100k tokens and science fiction about 14k; the smaller one has a higher TTR almost automatically.

choices.text: No — TTR can never be compared across texts.
choices.feedback: Too strong. It can be compared when the texts are the same length, or with a length-corrected measure.

hints: Recall what happens to TTR as a text gets longer. Then ask: are the two categories the same length?
The reflex is to accept a number because it's a number. The chapter's caveat (Alice vs Moby Dick) is exactly this case.
The fix is mechanical: sample equal-size windows from each, or use a size-corrected measure, and *then* compare.
solution: Not justified as stated. TTR decreases with text length because vocabulary grows as K·nᵝ with β < 1 — bigger corpus, lower ratio.
Check the token counts: in Brown, news ≈ 100,000 tokens, science fiction ≈ 14,000. The smaller category is expected to have a higher TTR regardless of style.
Instead: compute TTR on equal-size samples (first 10,000 tokens of each, or averaged over 10k windows), or use a length-corrected measure (MTLD, or a standardized TTR).
Then, if sci-fi is still higher, you can start to talk about vocabulary — and even then it's a claim about these texts, not about 'sci-fi authors'.
exercises.why: Comparing rates across groups of different sizes is the most common statistical mistake in any field — from 'this city has more crime' to 'this model has more errors'. Heaps' law is just the linguistics version. Catching it is what 'quantitative literacy' means.
